hero.caption: The whole gamble nearly turned into a second war right here: the USS *San Jacinto* throws a shot across the bow of the British mail packet *Trent* and a boarding party hauls off two Confederate envoys. The Union captain who pulled it off had no orders at all.
hero.credit: Popular Graphic Arts · hand-colored lithograph · pre-1931 · Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (pga.08085) · public domain

figs.caption: The North turned the seizure into a gleeful joke before it learned how angry London was: "Policeman Wilkes" nabs the well-known rogues Mason and Slidell as they try to pawn the Confederacy's goods at the shop of Bull & Crapaud. The celebration was a catastrophe in waiting.
figs.credit: *Harper's Weekly* · wood engraving · 1861 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
figs.heading: The *Trent* and the brink of a second war

figs.caption: The famine the South dreamed of actually arrived — just too late and aimed at the wrong people. Idled mill workers queue for their breakfast in a courtyard near Manchester. Many of these same hungry operatives would vote to back Lincoln and emancipation anyway.
figs.credit: *Illustrated London News* · wood engraving · 1862 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
figs.heading: A hunger in Lancashire

figs.caption: Lincoln's Secretary of State swung the threats. Seward told dinner guests the United States would "wrap the whole world in flames" before it let Europe recognize the South — and drafted a dispatch so hot that Lincoln had to personally tone it down.
figs.credit: Unknown photographer; restoration by Adam Cuerden · albumen print · 1859 · Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (cph.3a23003) · public domain
figs.heading: Seward wraps the world in flames

figs.caption: Half of the South's diplomatic A-team: James Mason of Virginia, sent to win over Britain. Snatched off the *Trent*, jailed, released — and then, for all the drama, he got exactly nothing out of London.
figs.credit: Mathew Brady studio · albumen print · c. 1855–1865 · Library of Congress, Brady-Handy Collection · public domain
figs.heading: The *Trent* and the brink of a second war

figs.caption: The other half: John Slidell of Louisiana, dispatched to charm France. Napoleon III received him warmly, dangled recognition for two years — and, like Mason, left him empty-handed.
figs.credit: Mathew Brady · albumen print · c. 1860 · Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (LCCN 2003663045) · public domain
figs.heading: The *Trent* and the brink of a second war

figs.caption: The man who almost started a second war single-handed. Wilkes stopped a neutral British ship on the high seas and dragged two passengers off it with no orders from anyone — a navy captain making foreign policy at gunpoint.
figs.credit: Unknown photographer · photograph · before 1877 · Smithsonian Institution (via Wikimedia Commons) · public domain
figs.heading: The *Trent* and the brink of a second war

figs.caption: If Europe wouldn't fight for the South, it would build for it. The British-made *CSS Alabama*, flying the stars and bars, burned roughly 65 Union merchant ships and never once entered a Confederate port — she lived her whole life on the open ocean.
figs.credit: Samuel Walters · oil on canvas · 1863 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
figs.heading: Ships built on the Mersey

figs.caption: The British Prime Minister who held the door shut. Palmerston flirted with mediation in the autumn of 1862, then insisted Russia come along first — which, since Russia leaned Union, was a polite way of insisting nothing happen at all.
figs.credit: Herbert Watkins · albumen carte-de-visite · 1857 · National Portrait Gallery, London (NPG x11978) · public domain
figs.heading: The autumn the door nearly opened

figs.caption: In October 1862 the Chancellor of the Exchequer stood up in Newcastle and all but crowned the Confederacy — "they have made a nation." Decades later he called it a blunder of "incredible grossness." He'd forgotten to ask what kind of nation he was endorsing: a slave state.
figs.credit: John Jabez Edwin Mayall · albumen carte-de-visite · 1861 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
figs.heading: The autumn the door nearly opened

figs.caption: The South's friendliest monarch — charming, scheming, and never quite committing. Napoleon III talked warmly of recognition for two years but would not move without Britain, and when Britain held back, so did he.
figs.credit: Alexandre Cabanel · oil on canvas · 1865 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
figs.heading: France: the Emperor who blew hot and cold

figs.caption: The Union's quiet winner. Son of one president and grandson of another — both ministers to Britain themselves — Adams kept Britain neutral through the *Trent* scare, the raiders, and the Laird rams. To Russell, on the rams: "this is war."
figs.credit: George Kendall Warren · photograph · 1861 · Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division (LCCN 2013651550) · public domain
figs.heading: The men who failed, and the men who held the line
